explanations.answer: The scourge will not touch them
explanations.explanation: That's their whole plan. They say, "When the overwhelming scourge passes through it will not touch us…" Then they tell you what they're leaning on: lies and falsehood. Friend, that's an oven mitt made of tissue paper, and nobody wants to be holding the hot pan with that.

The rulers never say a word about growing. Their words are about the overwhelming scourge passing through and not touching them. The deal is all about getting through the scourge untouched, not about getting bigger. Nobody in these verses is asking for a bigger bakery.
Being remembered isn't what they ask for. They say the overwhelming scourge "…will not touch us…" Their eyes are on getting past it, not on a legacy. Nobody in this verse is ordering a statue.

Right in the verse: "See, I lay a stone in Zion, a tested stone, a precious cornerstone, a sure foundation…" The Lord GOD names the place Himself. The rulers picked a hiding place of their own, and He answers with a stone He's laying.
Bethel is a real name, but it's not the one in this verse. The Lord GOD says, "See, I lay a stone in Zion…" So the stone goes in Zion. Hang on to that name, friend.
Shiloh doesn't show up in these words. The Lord GOD says, "See, I lay a stone in Zion…" That's where He puts the stone. Good guess on a place name, though, since the Bible is full of them.

That's what He says: "the one who believes will never be shaken." It comes right after the tested stone, the precious cornerstone, the sure foundation. I spent years in the back of a junk drawer, so believe me, a foundation that doesn't move sounds GOOD.
It's the other way around. The Lord GOD says, "the one who believes will never be shaken." That promise sits right beside the stone He lays in Zion. So the believer is the one who stays put.

The Lord GOD says, "Hail will sweep away your refuge of lies, and water will flood your hiding place." So the refuge of lies gets hail and the hiding place gets water. Their hiding place isn't built to hold up against either.

Fire is nowhere in this verse, and I would know, I keep a lot of ovens. The Lord GOD says, "Hail will sweep away your refuge of lies…" Water is what floods the hiding place. Two weather pictures, and neither one is fire.
No locusts here. The Lord GOD says, "Hail will sweep away your refuge of lies, and water will flood your hiding place." The sweeping comes from hail. Keep the bugs out of this one, friend.

The rulers hoped it would, but that's not what the Lord GOD says. He says, "Your covenant with death will be dissolved, and your agreement with Sheol will not stand." So the deal doesn't hold. It gets dissolved.

Yes, it's False. The Lord GOD says, "Your covenant with death will be dissolved, and your agreement with Sheol will not stand." That covenant is what the rulers said they had made. He says it comes apart.

The Lord GOD says, "When the overwhelming scourge passes through, you will be trampled by it." That's the opposite of what the rulers were counting on. I think this is one of the heavy parts of the passage, so I'll leave it right there.

Spared is what the rulers were hoping for. They said the scourge "…will not touch us…" But the Lord GOD says, "When the overwhelming scourge passes through, you will be trampled by it." I think this is a heavy line, so I'll let it stand.

The verse never says anything about being forgotten. The Lord GOD says, "When the overwhelming scourge passes through, you will be trampled by it." The word is trampled. It's a heavy line, and I won't dress it up.
The text says more than one time. The Lord GOD says, "As often as it passes through, it will carry you away…" It keeps coming. This isn't a one-time thing.

Right, it isn't just one time. The Lord GOD says, "As often as it passes through, it will carry you away; it will sweep through morning after morning, by day and by night." Morning after morning, day and night. It keeps coming back.
Isaiah says the LORD will rise up "…to do His work, His strange work, and to perform His task, His disturbing task." Those are the words the text gives. Isaiah doesn't soften them, so I won't either.

Isaiah picks different words. He says the LORD will rise up "…to do His work, His strange work, and to perform His task, His disturbing task." Strange and disturbing are the words in the verse. Gentle isn't one of them.
Not what Isaiah says. He calls it "…His strange work…" and "…His disturbing task." Strange means unusual, and disturbing means unsettling. Easy and expected aren't words you'll find in that verse.
Isaiah says, "So now, do not mock, or your shackles will become heavier." The mocking makes the shackles weigh more. It's a warning, and it comes with a way out: stop mocking.
The warning goes the other direction. Isaiah says, "So now, do not mock, or your shackles will become heavier." Heavier, not loose. The mocking is what makes them weigh more.
Rust isn't in the verse. Isaiah says, "So now, do not mock, or your shackles will become heavier." The shackles get heavier, not older. It's a warning to the scoffers to stop.

explanations.answer: He levels it and then plants
explanations.explanation: Isaiah says, "When he has leveled its surface, does he not sow caraway and scatter cumin?" The plowing has an end. When the ground is ready, the farmer plants. Work with a finish line, friend.

explanations.answer: He keeps plowing all year long
explanations.explanation: Isaiah's question is, "Does the plowman plow for planting every day?" He's asking it because the answer is no. The next verse says that when he has leveled the surface, he sows caraway and scatters cumin. Plowing all year long? Friend, even I would ask that man if he's okay.

explanations.answer: He leaves it to rest a year
explanations.explanation: Resting the field isn't what these verses say. Isaiah says, "When he has leveled its surface, does he not sow caraway and scatter cumin?" So the farmer levels the surface, and then he sows. A year off isn't in the picture.

Isaiah says the opposite. "He plants wheat in rows and barley in plots, and rye within its border." Rows, plots and a border, so each crop gets its own spot. One big pile of seed? That farmer would need a miracle and a very patient sorting crew.

Yes, it's False. Isaiah says, "He plants wheat in rows and barley in plots, and rye within its border." Rows for the wheat, plots for the barley, a border for the rye. The farmer keeps each crop in its place.
Isaiah says, "For his God instructs and teaches him properly." The farmer's know-how comes from God. Isaiah puts the teaching right there in the field.
A father could teach a farmer plenty, but that's not what the verse says. Isaiah says, "For his God instructs and teaches him properly." The teacher in the text is God.
The neighbor doesn't get the credit here. Isaiah says, "For his God instructs and teaches him properly." The farmer's God is the one doing the teaching.

Isaiah says, "But caraway is beaten out with a stick, and cumin with a rod." Right before that, he says caraway is not threshed with a sledge. So the sledge stays out of it, and the farmer reaches for a stick.

Isaiah doesn't use a millstone for the caraway. He says, "But caraway is beaten out with a stick, and cumin with a rod." Grinding comes up later, but that's for grain for bread (Isaiah 28:28). For the caraway, it's a stick.
A winnowing fork never shows up in these verses. Isaiah says, "But caraway is beaten out with a stick, and cumin with a rod." So the caraway gets a stick. Good guess on a farm tool, though.

That's right. Isaiah says, "Grain for bread must be ground, but it is not endlessly threshed." The farmer threshes it, but not endlessly. I'd be thrilled if my kneading ever came with a stopping point like that.
It's the other way around. Isaiah says, "Grain for bread must be ground, but it is not endlessly threshed." The threshing has a stopping point, and the farmer knows when to quit.

explanations.answer: Wonderful in counsel and excellent in wisdom
explanations.explanation: Isaiah says, "This also comes from the LORD of Hosts, who is wonderful in counsel and excellent in wisdom." The farmer's knowing when to plant, when to thresh and when to stop is a picture of that wisdom. The farmer is taught by God, and the wisdom is God's.

explanations.answer: Mighty in battle and fearsome in strength
explanations.explanation: That sounds like a fine description, but it's not the one Isaiah gives here. He says the LORD of Hosts is "…wonderful in counsel and excellent in wisdom." The verse comes right after a field full of careful, fitting work. So the words are about counsel and wisdom.

explanations.answer: Gracious in mercy and abounding in love
explanations.explanation: Those are lovely words, but they aren't the ones in this verse. Isaiah says the LORD of Hosts is "…wonderful in counsel and excellent in wisdom." That fits the whole farm picture, with the right tool for each seed. Counsel and wisdom are the words to remember here.
